comparison: Both strongly support the methodological approach and study design (C1, C2, C11-C14). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of HMM methodology and model selection criteria. Peer reviewers affirm the work as 'important' with 'state-of-the-art' methods and 'sound' methodology. Both evaluations are aligned in supporting the core methodological framework.

Both strongly support reproducibility findings (C3, C34, C90). OpenEval provides statistical validation (r=0.94, p<0.0001) while noting 'unprecedented reproducibility' is somewhat hyperbolic. Peer reviewers explicitly highlight reproducibility as a strength, with the editor emphasizing 'reliable transition structure.' Both agree this is a core strength, though OpenEval is more cautious about the superlative claim.

Both support the mapping of HMM states to PSG stages (C15-C21). OpenEval provides detailed validation of state assignments and discusses the absence of N1-specific states in relation to N1's poor inter-rater reliability. Peer reviewers accept these associations without challenge, noting the work 'advances our understanding' of brain states underlying sleep and wakefulness.

Both strongly support the identification of substates within N2 and REM (C24-C28, C56). OpenEval validates the modularity analysis and N2 subdivision through transition probabilities and EEG data. Peer reviewers explicitly state this provides 'the most compelling evidence on the sub-states of both REM and N2 sleep' and describe it as a fundamental finding. Strong agreement on this novel contribution.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN while peer reviewers SUPPORT the REM substates characterization (C4, C29, C61-C66). OpenEval distinguishes between well-supported empirical observations and speculative interpretation of tonic vs. phasic REM, noting the interpretation lacks direct validation. Peer reviewers praise the substate identification without questioning the tonic/phasic interpretation. Divergence in critical evaluation of interpretive claims.

Both support the distinction between pre- and post-sleep wake states (C30-C33). OpenEval validates this through multiple converging measures (temporal, physiological, transition probabilities). Peer reviewers accept the wake state characterization as part of the broader substate findings they praise. Agreement on this refinement beyond standard PSG staging.

Both support the temporal characterization and resolution advantages (C22-C23, C48-C50). OpenEval quantifies the 2.5-fold improvement over PSG's 30s epochs. Peer reviewers accept the temporal characterization and implicitly endorse finer temporal resolution as meaningful. Strong agreement on this methodological advantage.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN while peer reviewers SUPPORT the functional connectivity findings (C35-C38, C67, C92). OpenEval distinguishes between well-supported empirical observations and speculative interpretations about DMN-ACN's 'critical role,' noting causality is not established. Peer reviewers accept the FC analyses without critique, though suggest more EEG integration. Divergence in evaluating causal vs. correlational claims.

Both support the sensory network connectivity patterns (C39-C41). OpenEval validates the general wake/sleep connectivity patterns and notes the REM state 6 exception. Peer reviewers accept the FC characterization as adding 'additional insights.' Agreement on these empirical findings.

Both support the relationship between HMM states and PSG stages (C42, C91). OpenEval validates through high correlation of FC patterns within modules and similarity between HMM and PSG time courses. Peer reviewers accept the FC analyses and note they add insights. Agreement on internal validation of the HMM approach.

Both support the motion quality control data (C43-C45, C102). OpenEval validates expected patterns and high data retention rates as demonstrating methodological rigor. Peer reviewers describe the methodology as 'sound' and the dataset as a 'primary strength' without raising motion concerns. Agreement on data quality.

OpenEval SUPPORTS while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN regarding EEG validation (C46-C47). OpenEval validates the EEG findings as providing cross-modal support for state assignments and N2 subdivisions. Peer reviewers identify a 'missed opportunity,' requesting complete EEG spectra for all 21 states and band-specific analyses for slow oscillation and sigma/spindle bands. Divergence on completeness of EEG characterization.

Both support the methodological advantages of the HMM approach (C48, C51-C53). OpenEval validates each advantage empirically (temporal resolution, spatial coverage, automation, transition modeling). Peer reviewers affirm the methodology as 'sound' and state conclusions are 'generally well-supported.' Agreement on methodological contributions.

Both support the acknowledgment of study limitations (C73-C76, C79). OpenEval notes limitations are appropriate and do not invalidate findings. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the small sample size as a weakness but conclude the evidence is 'convincing' and conclusions 'generally well-supported.' Agreement that limitations are appropriately acknowledged and do not undermine core findings.

OpenEval SUPPORTS while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN regarding EEG method generalizability (C77-C78). OpenEval finds the potential EEG application reasonable given HMM is a general time-series method. Peer reviewers identify 'absence of more analyses relating the HMM states back to EEG' as a missed opportunity, suggesting analyses that might reveal novel EEG changes. Divergence on whether EEG integration is adequate or incomplete.

OpenEval supports the comparison to prior work (C80-C82), noting the methodological advance of capturing full sleep cycles including REM, which 1-hour recordings cannot achieve. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific comparison to Stevner et al.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the salience network restoration hypothesis (C68-C72), noting it is explicitly speculative and lacks direct evidence from the current study. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific theoretical interpretation.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the clinical application potential (C93), noting it is aspirational rather than demonstrated and requires validation in patient populations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing future clinical applications.

OpenEval supports the comprehensive methodological documentation (C94-C104, C112-C113) as meeting reproducibility standards. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the completeness of methodological reporting, though peer reviewers implicitly accept methodology as adequate.
